prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map captures the continuous 3D geometry of a wooden-floored room containing no people, starting with a dark couch/armrest on the far left within arm's reach (~0.3–0.6 m), a wicker basket (~0.8–1.0 m), and a small green child's table with a wooden stool tucked in front of it (~1.0–1.5 m) and a red-slatted chair behind it against the left wall, followed by a grey shelf (~2–3 m) and a full-sized dining table with chairs to the right (~3–4 m away, ~2 m across from the left wall). Across the 5 frames, the camera wearer steps back and pans right from the close left corner (frames 1–2), causing a motion-blurred transition in frame 3 before revealing the wider floor, rug at the bottom left (~0.5–1.0 m), and distant dining area as the child's table shifts to the far left at ~1.5–2.5 m (frames 4–5). In frames 1 and 2, the couch edge, basket, and near edge of the child's table are within or just at the camera wearer's arm's reach (<1 m), while the stool partially occludes the table legs and the left furniture is partially cropped at the frame borders. Compared to the dimly lit RGB frames, the depth map clearly separates the dark foreground couch edge and wicker basket from the shadowed wall in frames 1–2 and preserves the geometric silhouettes of the tables during severe motion blur in frame 3. However, the map is unreliable on fine open structures, filling in the gaps between the red chair's slats and between the distant dining table legs as solid dark or mid-grey planes.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map fails to capture the overall room layout and detects objects in only three of the five frames, leaving frames 1 and 3 completely blank due to dark lighting and severe motion blur. In frame 2, it segments the child's green table and front wooden stool together as a single 'dining table' (~1.0–1.5 m away on the left), the red-slatted backrest above and behind it as a 'chair' (~1.3 m), and a small white container on the grey shelf behind the table to the right as a 'cup' (~2.2 m). In frames 4 and 5, as the camera turns right and retreats so the child's table is ~2 m away on the left, the map misses the foreground rug and shelf entirely, detecting only a distant 'chair' under the right dining table (~3.5 m) in frame 4, and the red-slatted 'chair' back on the left (~2.2 m), a 'bowl' on the shelf (~3.0 m), and the distant right 'chair' (~3.5 m) in frame 5. The map also produces a false-positive 'person' mask on the dark side of the wooden stool/table leg (~1.5 m away on the left) in frame 4, even though no people are present in the scene to face or look toward the camera wearer or reach any objects. While segmentation isolates the small white container/bowl on the cluttered shelf and the distant chair legs against the dark background in frames 2, 4, and 5, it is highly unreliable across the sequence, dropping almost all furniture, merging the child's table and stool, and misclassifying shadowed wood as a person.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is completely black across all 5 frames, detecting no yellow body skeletons or magenta hand skeletons anywhere in the sequence. Using the RGB strip for context, this absence of detections accurately reflects that no other people are present in the room—only furniture arranged along the left wall (~0.3–3.0 m away) and the right dining area (~3.0–4.5 m away)—so there is no one facing or looking toward the camera wearer. Although the camera wearer's own body is out of view behind the head-mounted camera as they turn right and step back from the close left corner (where the couch edge and basket are within ~0.3–0.8 m arm's reach in frames 1–2), a tiny white edge at the very bottom-left corner of frame 5 on the rug (~0.5 m below the camera) is not registered as a body part. Compared to the segmentation map, which falsely labels a shadowed table/stool leg as a person in frame 4, the pose map usefully confirms the absence of any human figures or articulated limbs in the dimly lit and motion-blurred room. However, because it relies entirely on visible human keypoints, the pose map provides zero information about the spatial layout, object distances, occlusions, or camera motion across the 5 frames.
